title: Timing an Enzyme with a Beam of Light

scenes.tts: Velocity is a slope: product formed per unit time. So you can only measure an enzyme by watching a reaction run. Doubling the substrate does not keep doubling the rate. Enzymes saturate, and the velocity levels off toward V max.
scenes.visual: Substrate and product in a flask with a question mark; bars for rate at 1, 2, 4 units of substrate that stop doubling and level toward a Vmax line.
scenes.caption: Velocity is a slope: product formed per unit time. So you can only measure an enzyme by watching a reaction run. Doubling the substrate does not keep doubling the rate. Enzymes saturate, and the velocity levels off toward Vmax.
scenes.narration: Velocity is a slope: product formed per unit time. So you can only measure an enzyme by watching a reaction run. Doubling the substrate does not keep doubling the rate. Enzymes saturate, and the velocity levels off toward Vmax.

scenes.tts: Pick a reaction where something absorbs light. N A D H absorbs at three hundred forty nanometres. N A D plus does not. So a dehydrogenase that makes or uses N A D H can be followed by its light. If your enzyme does not touch N A D H, couple it to one that does. Pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate, and lactate dehydrogenase then consumes N A D H, so the absorbance falls.
scenes.visual: A cuvette in a beam of 340 nm light, NADH makes the beam dim and NAD+ does not; then a two-step chain: pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate, lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH, the reading falls.
scenes.caption: Pick a reaction where something absorbs light. NADH absorbs at 340 nanometres. NAD+ does not. So a dehydrogenase that makes or uses NADH can be followed by its light. If your enzyme does not touch NADH, couple it to one that does. Pyruvate kinase makes pyruvate, and lactate dehydrogenase then consumes NADH, so the absorbance falls.

scenes.tts: Mix buffer, coenzyme and enzyme, then add substrate to start. Record the absorbance at short intervals, for example every five to ten seconds for sixty seconds. Stay in the instrument's linear range. Beer-Lambert turns that change into a change in concentration: divide by epsilon times path length. For N A D H, epsilon is six thousand two hundred twenty per molar per centimetre.
scenes.visual: Components pour into the cuvette, a timer starts, dots of A340 appear every few seconds on a falling curve inside a marked linear range; the Beer-Lambert line appears with epsilon and path length.
scenes.caption: Mix buffer, coenzyme and enzyme, then add substrate to start. Record the absorbance at short intervals, for example every 5 to 10 seconds for 60 seconds. scenes.tts: Take the slope of the straight early part of the curve. That is the initial velocity. Measure it at many substrate concentrations, holding all else fixed. Each slope is one point on a curve: steep at low substrate, flattening toward V max. Fit the curve by nonlinear regression. K m is the substrate concentration at half V max.
scenes.visual: Progress curves at several substrate levels with initial slopes drawn; each slope becomes a dot on a rate-versus-substrate plot; the hyperbola fits through them; Vmax and half-Vmax mark Km.
scenes.caption: Take the slope of the straight early part of the curve. That is the initial velocity. Measure it at many substrate concentrations, holding all else fixed. scenes.tts: Idealised example: V max is sixty micromoles per minute and K m is four millimolar. At twelve millimolar the rate is forty-five, three quarters of V max. In the Lineweaver-Burk plot, one over v against one over S, the y intercept is one over V max and the x intercept minus one over K m. A competitive inhibitor keeps V max and raises apparent K m: lines share a y intercept. An uncompetitive one gives parallel lines. A noncompetitive one lowers V max and keeps K m: lines share the x intercept.
scenes.visual: Idealised curve with the worked point at 12 mM reaching 45; then the double-reciprocal line with intercepts marked; three small panels show competitive, uncompetitive, noncompetitive line families.
scenes.caption: Idealised example: Vmax is 60 micromoles per minute and Km is 4 millimolar. At 12 millimolar the rate is 45, three quarters of Vmax. In the Lineweaver-Burk plot, 1/v against 1/S, the y intercept is 1/Vmax and the x intercept −1/Km. A competitive inhibitor keeps Vmax and raises apparent Km: lines share a y intercept. An uncompetitive one gives parallel lines. A noncompetitive one lowers Vmax and keeps Km: lines share the x intercept.

scenes.tts: Not an initial rate: as substrate is used and product builds, product can inhibit the enzyme or run the reaction backward. Measure only the early linear stretch. The usual rule: less than ten percent of the substrate should be consumed; read for less time or use less enzyme. The straight-line plot weights errors unequally and compresses the most accurate data. Fit the curve, use the line only to see the pattern.
scenes.visual: Three panels build: a curve bending away from its tangent (use only the early stretch); a substrate bar with a 10 percent mark (shorten the read or lower enzyme); a double-reciprocal plot with the high-substrate points crowded together, versus the hyperbola fit.

Fit the curve, use the line only to see the pattern.

scenes.tts: Michaelis and Menten, in 1913, built their equation from initial velocities of invertase at several sucrose concentrations, measuring the rate by optical rotation. In the 1930s, Warburg and Christian, with a more sensitive spectrometer, showed that N A D and N A D P differ in absorption between their reduced and oxidised forms. That made the optical test for dehydrogenases.
scenes.visual: Two cards build with source tags: 1913 rate by optical rotation, v-versus-S curve; 1930s two absorbance spectra for reduced versus oxidised coenzyme (idealised sketch), then a dehydrogenase labelled optical test.
scenes.caption: Michaelis and Menten, in 1913, built their equation from initial velocities of invertase at several sucrose concentrations, measuring the rate by optical rotation. In the 1930s, Warburg and Christian, with a more sensitive spectrometer, showed that NAD and NADP differ in absorption between their reduced and oxidised forms. That made the optical test for dehydrogenases.

scenes.tts: A G six P D deficiency test on red cells reads the rise in A340 as N A D P plus becomes N A D P H. It guards against haemolysis from oxidative drugs such as primaquine. In 1977, Chacko, Conti and Adelstein found smooth-muscle myosin had a higher actin-activated A T Pase once its light chain was phosphorylated: a change in measured enzyme rate. Remember: K m is not simply affinity. It approximates the dissociation constant only when catalysis is slow compared with substrate falling off.
scenes.visual: G6PD rising A340 trace card; a myosin ATPase rate bar rising after phosphorylation; then the rule box: Km is not simply affinity, with the hedge.
